terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Build the bill here and run it, after you call your functions from main.

tasks.title: Price the labour
tasks.description:
Ambrose charges 48 an hour, counted by the minute. Under `// Task 1` in `src/bill.cpp`, above `main`, write a function called `labourCost` that takes the minutes worked as an `int` and gives back what they cost as a `double`. 90 minutes cost 72.

Check calls `labourCost` from code of its own with other minutes, and reads what it gives back and what it prints. It gives the cost back; it prints nothing.
nextSteps: Write the first line: what it gives back, its name, and its parameter in round brackets.
Inside its `{ }`, work out the cost from the parameter.
End with a `return` of the cost.
Call it from `main` with 90 and print what it gives back, then build and run.
hints: A function starts with the type of what it gives back, then its name, then its parameters with their types: `double labourCost(...)`.
48 an hour is 48 for 60 minutes. Two whole numbers divided give a whole number, so write one of them as a `double`, like `60.0`, before you divide.
The shape is `double labourCost(int minutes) { return minutes * 48.0 / 60; }`.

tasks.title: Print a line of the bill
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, write a function called `printBillLine` that takes what the line is for as a `std::string` and the amount as a `double`, prints them as one line and gives nothing back:

```
Mainspring: 18.5
```

Check calls `printBillLine` from code of its own with other lines, and reads what it prints.
nextSteps: Write the first line with `void` in front: it gives nothing back.
Give it two parameters, separated by a comma, each with its type.
Inside, print the line from the two parameters, and end it.
Call it from `main` with a line of your own, build and run.
hints: A function that gives nothing back has `void` where the type of the result would be, and needs no `return`.
Parameters are separated by commas, and each has its own type: `(std::string what, double amount)`. Print them with `std::cout`, the colon and the space as text between them.
The shape is `void printBillLine(std::string what, double amount) { std::cout << what << ": " << amount << "\n"; }`.

tasks.title: Add up a repair
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, write a function called `repairTotal` that takes the minutes worked as an `int` and the cost of the parts as a `double`, and gives back the whole price as a `double`: the labour plus the parts. Work out the labour by calling `labourCost`.

Check calls `repairTotal` with other minutes and parts, and reads what it gives back and whether it called `labourCost`. Check gives it a `labourCost` of its own, so this task does not depend on Task 1.
nextSteps: Write the first line, with its two parameters.
Give back the labour plus the parts.
Call it from `main`, print the result, build and run.
hints: A function can call another function that is written above it, just as `main` can.
`labourCost(minutes)` is a value, the one it gives back, so it can stand in a sum like any number.
The shape is `double repairTotal(int minutes, double parts) { return labourCost(minutes) + parts; }`.

tasks.title: Round the minutes up to a quarter hour
tasks.description:
Ambrose bills whole quarter hours. Under `// Task 4`, write a function called `minutesToBill` that takes the minutes worked as an `int` and gives back, as an `int`, the minutes rounded up to the next quarter hour: 50 gives 60, 60 stays 60, and 61 gives 75.

Check calls `minutesToBill` with other minutes, and reads what it gives back and its own minutes after the call: they must stay as they were.
nextSteps: Write the first line: an `int` in, an `int` back.
Decide how to tell whether the minutes are already a whole number of quarter hours.
While they are not, move them up a minute, then give them back.
Call it from `main` with 50, 60 and 61, build and run.
hints: `minutes % 15` is 0 exactly when the minutes are a whole number of quarter hours.
The parameter is a copy of the caller's value, so the function may change it on the way: a loop can add 1 to it until it is a whole number of quarter hours.
The shape is `while (minutes % 15 != 0) { minutes++; }`, then `return minutes;`.
